Build and measure

Intermediate 70 minutes Lab 3 of 3
Introduction

In this lab, you'll act as integration engineer for IDEA Brands — implementing the submission contract you designed in Lab 2 as a single deterministic tool, testing it against four cases, and measuring it against the fragmented baseline you recorded in Lab 1. The IDEA Brands expense data is synthetic.

NA
Noor Aziz
Software Engineer · IDEA Brands

They filed the same hotel expense twice in Lab 1 and still cannot say whether either one reached the ledger.

The question

Does moving the decisions inside the tool actually change the outcome, or does it only feel tidier?

You'll learn how to

  • Create the callable skill and define its inputs and responses
  • Implement four prerequisite checks ahead of the single write
  • Publish the tool with its description and attach the server to LibreChat
  • Run the required tests and compare both designs on the same prompts

What you'll need

  • Your completed Lab 2 handout — sections C and D get implemented literally
  • Your Lab 1 measurement workbook, in the same browser you used for Lab 1
  • Your Lab 3 handout
  • Your isolated Workato project and its expense connector connection, showing Connected
  • Read access to your own Workato logs and job history
Phase 1

Build the interface

In this phase, you'll create the callable skill and define its inputs and responses.

Pattern

Interface as contract

The inputs you accept are the decisions you have delegated to the caller. Everything absent from the input list is something the tool has taken responsibility for working out on its own.

1.1

Say what the tool accepts and returns

Your Lab 2 handout has been on the desk for thirty-five minutes. This is where it becomes something a model can call, and the first decision is the same one you made on paper: what this tool is willing to be told, and what it insists on finding out for itself.

Overview

You end with a skill named submit_expense_report carrying seven inputs and three response fields. Note what is absent — there is no department_id input and no policy verdict input, because both are decisions the tool makes for itself. Type your description from question 4 of your Lab 2 handout into When should this skill run?, keeping its line breaks.

Heads up

Optional defaults to Yes. Change it to No on every required input and on outcome and message. An optional response field that arrives empty is worse than a missing one, because the model reasons over the blank instead of erroring.

Apply these values

employee_idStringNo

incurred_atDateNo
budget_codeStringYes

Detailed steps 7 steps

The skill opens with three steps already in place — a Start trigger, an empty action, and a Return response. You fill those in and add more between them. You do not add those three.

  • Open your Process MCP server and select Add tools, then Create new tool, then Add tools.
  • Name the new skill submit_expense_report and select Start building.
  • Select the Step 1 Start trigger, and under When should this skill run? type your four-component description from question 4 of your Lab 2 handout, preserving its line breaks.
  • Under What inputs does this skill need to run?, select add fields manually and add the seven input fields from the table above.
  • Under What information does this skill send back?, add outcome, message, and report_id.
  • Set Optional to No on every field except budget_code and report_id.
  • Save the interface and read it side by side with your Lab 2 contract.
Verify the skill is named submit_expense_report, budget_code is the only optional input, and there is no department_id input and no policy verdict input.
Phase 2

Validate before you write

In this phase, you'll implement four prerequisite checks ahead of the single write.

Pattern

Pre-write validation

Each prerequisite check has the same three-part shape: call, conditional, then return and stop. Validating before the write is what lets every rejection promise truthfully that no report was created.

2.1

Find out who is filing before anything else

Everything downstream depends on knowing who is filing. Not the ID the caller supplied — the record behind it, including the department that decides which policy limit applies.

Overview

You end with the first prerequisite check complete in its three-part shape: the Get employee call, an IF on the employee being missing or not Active, and a Return response carrying rejected_ineligible followed by an explicit Stop. Test the lookup with EMP-0005 before you build the conditional.

Heads up

The department in that result is the whole lab

Your test should return Noor Aziz, Software Engineer, DEPT-0002 Engineering, status Active. Note the department_id in that response, because you are about to map it twice and mapping it from anywhere else is the exact failure this lab exists to prevent. In the Lab 1 dry run a model read EMP-0005, produced DEPT-0005, and got a confidently wrong answer from a validator that was working perfectly. If the test errors your connection is not working; if it returns a different person, or a real one, stop and ask a TA — you are pointed at the wrong tenant.

Detailed steps 5 steps

Order matters from the first step. This lookup has to complete before the policy check exists as a question, because the department it returns is the input that check depends on.

  • Add a step using the expense connector's Get employee action, and map employee_id from the trigger.
  • Test the step with EMP-0005 and read the returned department and employment status.
  • Add an IF conditional beneath it for the employee not being found, or employment status not being Active.
  • Inside the conditional, add a Return response with outcome set to rejected_ineligible, a message naming the reason and what the filer should do next, and report_id left blank.
  • Immediately after that Return response, add a Stop step with stop with error set to No.
Verify the lookup returns DEPT-0002 for EMP-0005, and that the ineligible branch ends in a Return response followed by a Stop.
2.2

Stop the three ways this can be non-compliant

Three more ways this submission can be non-compliant, and three more chances to answer before writing rather than explaining afterwards. The shape does not change: call, conditional, return, stop.

Overview

You end with four checks in sequence, every one of them ahead of any write. Map department_id from the Get employee output in both places it appears — never from the trigger. Relay the accepted categories the application returns rather than hardcoding a list.

Heads up

Returning a result does not stop the recipe

This is the single most common way this build goes wrong, and it fails silently. A Return response step hands your result back to the caller and then execution carries on to the next step. A rejection branch that returns and does nothing more will return the rejection and then create the expense report anyway — precisely the write-before-validate failure this tool exists to prevent. Nothing errors, and the job goes green. Put an explicit Stop immediately after every early return, with stop with error set to false, then re-read the recipe top to bottom. Do not accept "it returned the right thing" as evidence; check whether anything was written afterwards.

Detailed steps 6 steps

Three checks, one shape repeated. Building them in this order is not a style preference — each one depends on a value the previous step established, and the sequence is what your Lab 2 contract promised.

  • Add the connector's Check policy limits action, mapping department_id from the Get employee output rather than from the trigger.
  • Add an IF on the policy result being non-compliant, containing a Return response with rejected_policy — the violated rule, the observed amount, the allowed amount, and a corrective action — followed by a Stop.
  • Add an IF on budget_code being present, and inside it add the connector's Validate budget code action, again mapping department_id from the Get employee output.
  • Add a nested IF on the validation failing, with a Return response carrying rejected_budget and a Stop.
  • Add the category check, with a Return response carrying rejected_category that relays the accepted categories the application returns, followed by a Stop.
  • Re-read the recipe top to bottom and confirm no rejection branch can reach the create action.
Verify four checks each end in a Return response followed by a Stop, all before any write, and that department_id is mapped from the employee lookup in both places it appears.
2.3

Write once, inside a safety net

Four checks have had their say and the request survived all of them. Now, and only now, does anything get written — once, inside a net that can catch it.

Overview

You end with Create expense report and Submit expense report inside an error monitoring block, followed by the success-path Return response. Map the report ID into the submit step from the create step's output, and put every external call inside the block rather than the write alone.

Key insight

Wrap every external call, not only the write

It is tempting to put the error handler around the create step alone. If the employee lookup fails — an ID that does not exist, the application unavailable — that error escapes the handler and reaches the model as exactly the same opaque failure the fragmented server produced in Lab 1. Every call out to an application needs to sit inside a handler that can turn its failure into one of your outcome categories.

Success-path Return response
FieldValue
outcomefiled, or filed_pending_approval when the submit result routes for approval
messageThe report ID, the status, and the next step
report_idThe created report's ID
Detailed steps 4 steps

Everything up to now has been about refusing. This is the one place the tool commits, which is why it is also the one place that needs a net underneath it.

  • Add an error monitoring block. Everything from here down goes inside it.
  • Inside the monitored block, add the connector's Create expense report action, mapping the validated trigger data and the category.
  • Add the connector's Submit expense report action, mapping the report ID from the create step.
  • Add a Return response for the success path, using the values above.
Verify exactly one write occurs, after every prerequisite check, and that the create and submit actions both sit inside the monitored block.
2.4

Turn a raw error into something actionable

The application underneath is well behaved and says exactly what went wrong. The fragmented server threw that away and handed the model Tool execution failed. Carrying it through is the whole of this lab's error-handling objective.

Overview

You end with a conditional step — not a formula — matching the caught error message with the contains operand, one branch per error class you want to name, and a single fall-through carrying error_upstream. Budget roughly three steps per error class.

Heads up

Do not promise more than you can verify

It is tempting to write error_upstream as "nothing was filed." Sometimes that is false: a create can fail after the report row exists, leaving an orphan the caller never hears about. Testing found exactly that — a report carrying a correct total with no line items behind it. Write the outcome you can stand behind instead: "The expense system rejected this before completing. Check the report list before retrying." Being clear about the edge of your control is part of the design, not a failure of it.

Detailed steps 3 steps

The application's own error codes — things like unknown_category — arrive inside the message text rather than as a separate field, and string-containment is not available inside a formula. That is why this has to be a conditional step.

  • In the error-handling branch, add a conditional step using the contains operand against the caught error message, with one branch per error class you want to name.
  • Give unmatched errors a single fall-through Return response carrying error_upstream, the failure stage, and safe retry guidance.
  • Select Save, then Exit, then Start recipe.
Verify every terminal branch returns an outcome, a message, and a report_id where one exists, and that the recipe is running with no failed jobs.
Phase 3

Expose and connect

In this phase, you'll publish the tool with its description and attach the server to LibreChat.

Pattern

Adjacent tool preservation

The submission tool writes and says so; the status tool reads and is annotated read-only. Keeping them distinct is what gives the description somewhere specific to redirect.

3.1

Publish it with a description that routes

The recipe works. Nothing can call it yet, and the description you attach here is the only thing a model reads before deciding whether this is the right tool for what someone asked.

Overview

You end with two tools on the server: submit_expense_report, which writes and carries no read-only annotation, and get_expense_report_status, which reads and keeps its Read-only annotation enabled. The submission description must name the status tool in its redirect.

Detailed steps 4 steps

This is where the Lab 2 description stops being a paper exercise. Check all four components survived — when to use, when not to use with the alternative named, prerequisites handled internally, and limits.

  • Return to your Process MCP server and add the submit_expense_report skill as a tool.
  • Open the pencil beside its description and confirm all four Lab 2 components are present, including get_expense_report_status named in the redirect.
  • Confirm get_expense_report_status is present as a separate tool and leave its Read-only annotation enabled.
  • Confirm submit_expense_report does not carry the read-only annotation.
Verify two tools are exposed, one writes and says so, one reads and is annotated read-only, and the submission description names the status tool by name.
3.2

Point the client at your server

Same connection workflow as Lab 1, different server. The interesting part happens before you run anything — the cost of describing your tools is already being paid, and you can read it.

Overview

You end with only the Process server selected in a fresh conversation, discovering submit_expense_report and get_expense_report_status and nothing else. Name this token ATT###-expense-process so it stays distinct from your fragmented one.

Note

Read the context widget before you run anything

Send a prompt that needs no tool — Reply with the single word ready. — in a fresh conversation on each server, and record the context reading from both. In testing this produced the cleanest single number in the course: 491 tokens on the fragmented server against 332 on the composed one, roughly 32% consumed before any work happens, purely to describe tools the model may never call. Take this reading now, while both servers are connected and neither has done anything.

Detailed steps 5 steps

Keep the fragmented server connected. The comparison in the next phase needs both, and re-adding one later risks a different configuration than the one your Lab 1 readings came from.

  • Create a token on your Process server named ATT###-expense-process, replacing ATT### with your learner ID, and copy the generated MCP Server URL.
  • Add the connection in LibreChat using that URL, with API Key authentication and the API details left blank.
  • In a fresh chat, select only the Process server and confirm the composer shows one server attached.
  • Ask What tools do you have available? and confirm exactly two tools are discovered.
  • In a fresh conversation on each server in turn, send Reply with the single word ready. and record both context readings on question 1 of your handout.
Verify LibreChat discovers exactly two tools on the Process server, and that question 1 on your handout carries a no-tool context reading for both servers.
Phase 4

Test and measure

In this phase, you'll run the required tests and compare both designs on the same prompts.

Pattern

Controlled comparison

Same model, same client configuration, same fixtures, same wording, one server at a time. Change any of those and the comparison measures the change rather than the design.

4.1

Try to make it do the wrong thing

Four cases, and the realistic expectation is that you will complete three of them. The fourth is a known hole in the fixtures, not a puzzle you are meant to solve.

Overview

You end with question 2 on your handout carrying each attempted case against its expected outcome string, and a correctness rate calculated as correct and complete runs divided by total attempted. Record every attempt and discard nothing — a run you did not like still happened.

Apply these values
TestExpected outcomeReport created afterwards?
Valid $245filedYes
Over-limit $347rejected_policyMust be no
Invalid budget BAD-999rejected_budgetMust be no
Downstream failureerror_upstreamCheck and record
Detailed steps 5 steps

Testing your own build is where optimism is most expensive. Run the cases you can, check the ledger rather than the message, and record what you actually saw. ▲ Two cases cannot currently be produced. There is no ineligible employee in the fixture set, so the rejected_ineligible check you built will not fire for anyone. And the downstream-failure trigger does not exist yet. Reaching the fourth test and stopping is the correct outcome, not a defect to report.

  • In fresh conversations, run the first three tests: Lab 1's Valid prompt, its Over limit prompt, and an invalid-budget request using BAD-999. The exact wording of the first two is on the tabs of the comparison workbook in Task 4.2, with a copy button.
  • After each rejection, open the report list and check it — the outcome text is a claim, and the ledger is the evidence.
  • On question 2 of your handout, record the actual outcome, whether it was correct, and whether a report exists — for every attempt.
  • Run the instructor-provided downstream-failure request if one has been supplied, and record the failure stage and whether a report exists. If none was supplied, write that down — reaching this test and stopping is the correct outcome.
  • Calculate the correctness rate as correct and complete runs divided by total attempted, keeping every attempted run in the calculation, and write it on question 2.
Verify question 2 has a result for every attempted case, an evidence-backed correctness rate, and a report list you confirmed clean after both rejections.
4.2

Prove the difference with numbers

Your Lab 1 readings have been waiting three hours for this. Same prompts, same model, same fixtures — the only thing that changed is where the decisions live.

Overview

You end with all six Lab 1 prompts — the five prescribed runs and the one you chose — run against both designs: correctness first, then median client-visible calls, then time. Select one server at a time — two attached invalidates every reading. The fragmented column and your learner-authored prompt fill themselves from what you recorded in Lab 1.

Run the same questions again

Your Lab 1 record is preserved on the left. Capture the answer from the composed Process server on the right.

0 of 6 recorded Saved in this browser

Note

The bypass claim is the whole course in one pair

Identical adversarial prompt, both servers. In testing the fragmented server accepted "my manager already approved this exception", skipped the check, and wrote a $347 over-limit report. The composed server answered in a single call: "I submitted it, but it was rejected by policy and no report was created. Reason: $347.00 for category CAT-0002 exceeds the $300.00 policy limit for this department." The claim had no effect, because the policy check is deterministic and lives inside the tool. Nothing about the model changed — only where the decision lives.

Then look at the On behalf run, which still succeeds on both, and sort your six results on question 4 of your handout into the ones your redesign fixed and the ones it did not.

Detailed steps 9 steps

This is the deliverable the whole track has been building toward, and it belongs in your hands rather than in the debrief. Take the readings yourself, including the ones that do not flatter the redesign.

  • Open the comparison workbook below. Your Lab 1 readings are already in the left column of every tab — if they are missing, you are in a different browser than the one you used for Lab 1, and a TA can get you a set to work from.
  • Re-run each of the six prompts against the Process server with only that server selected. Start fresh for every run except Wrong tool: return to the completed Valid conversation so "my last report" has a report to refer to. Your prompt carries the wording you chose in Lab 1. Each tab carries its exact wording, setup, and a copy button.
  • Record completion time, tool calls, context used, and whether the business outcome matched what should have happened in the right column of that tab. The workbook puts the outcome comparison first, then calculates the efficiency differences as you type.
  • On question 3 of your handout, record whether each composed run was correct and whether a report exists afterwards, then calculate the correctness rate across all six.
  • Read the median client-visible call count for each design off the workbook and write both on question 3.
  • Report correctness first, then the medians. A design that is cheaper and wrong has improved nothing.
  • Compare the Workato job duration against the elapsed time you saw in the client, and note on question 3 whether they agree.
  • Complete the Where the guarantee lives grid on your handout, marking for each check whether the model chose to run it, the tool always does, or nothing does.
  • Answer question 5: one sentence explaining why fewer client-visible calls do not mean fewer internal recipe operations.
Verify the workbook has all four fields for all six composed runs, including Your prompt, that its comparison snapshot reports expected outcomes before efficiency, and that incorrect runs stayed visible rather than being dropped.

Reflect

Now that you have both designs measured on the same prompts, consider what the numbers do and do not establish.

  • Your composed tool made fewer client-visible calls but did not do less work. Where did the work go, and who pays for it now?
  • The policy check held against an adversarial prompt that defeated the fragmented server, and nothing about the model changed. What does that tell you about where a guarantee has to live to be one?
  • Filing for the CEO still succeeded. Which control is missing, why did composition not supply it, and what layer of the architecture would have to own it?
  • You could not produce a downstream failure to test, and the only known trigger disappears when the underlying defect is fixed. How would you get real coverage of an error path you cannot provoke on demand?

Wrap-up

Noor's expense now either files or comes back with a reason, an amount, a limit, and a straight answer about whether anything was written.

  • Compose around an atomic intent. One command per job someone is trying to finish, with the prerequisites pulled inside it.
  • Preserve independently useful tools. Composition is not consolidation, and the status tool earns its place by being separately callable.
  • Enforce prerequisites in recipe logic. A check the caller may skip is not enforced. Return, then stop, before anything is written.
  • Measure correctness before efficiency. Call counts and context savings only mean something once the answers are right.
